```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

# Introduction

The `mtcars` data set ships with R: 32 cars from the 1974 *Motor Trend*
magazine, with fuel consumption and ten aspects of design. This report asks
one question: **how much does weight cost in miles per gallon?**

> Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler.

# Data

```{r glimpse}
mtcars %>%
  select(mpg, cyl, hp, wt) %>%
  head()
```

The variables used here:

- `mpg`: miles per US gallon
- `cyl`: number of cylinders
- `hp`: gross horsepower
- `wt`: weight in thousands of pounds

Cars have between `r min(mtcars$cyl)` and `r max(mtcars$cyl)` cylinders, and
the median car weighs `r round(median(mtcars$wt) * 1000)` pounds.

# Weight against fuel economy

```{r scatter, fig.cap="Heavier cars burn more fuel", fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "Miles per gallon", colour = "Cylinders")
```

A linear model puts a number on the slope:

```{r model}
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
coef(summary(fit))
```

Each extra thousand pounds costs about `r round(abs(coef(fit)[2]), 1)` miles
per gallon. The fitted line is

$$\widehat{\text{mpg}} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{wt}$$

# By cylinder count

```{r table}
mtcars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarise(cars = n(), mpg = mean(mpg), hp = mean(hp)) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Averages per cylinder count")
```

| Cylinders | Typical use            |
|-----------|------------------------|
| 4         | Economy cars           |
| 6         | Mid-size sedans        |
| 8         | Muscle cars and trucks |
